breaking.headline: Anthropic prices IPO at $83, above its $70–$78 range
breaking.fact: Anthropic priced its IPO on Wednesday at $83 a share, well above the $70–$78 range it had targeted, with the offering upsized to meet heavy demand and the valuation set north of $1.4 trillion. Shares debut on the Nasdaq on Thursday under the ticker ANT.

breaking.headline: Fed minutes point to a near-certain December hike
breaking.fact: Minutes from the Fed’s October meeting showed nearly all participants favored a rate hike in December, and a couple said an increase of more than 25 basis points could warrant consideration if inflation data disappoint. Fed Governor Christopher Waller said Wednesday the Fed may need a half-point move to remind markets that 3% is not the inflation target.

breaking.headline: Pending home sales fall to a record low
breaking.fact: Pending sales of existing U.S. homes fell to a new record low in October as high mortgage rates squeezed demand: the National Association of Realtors’ index of contract signings dropped 4.7% to 63, its lowest reading since records began in 2001, and is down about 17% from a year earlier.

breaking.headline: Copper plunges as much as 5.6%, lowest since April
breaking.fact: Copper plunged in a broad selloff across London, New York and Shanghai, falling as much as 5.6% on the London Metal Exchange to its lowest since April, as investors bailed on bets tied to the AI boom and turned outright bearish even as extreme squeezes roil metals markets. Tin, another key AI-industry input, also shed value.

weekInBrief.headline: Trump lands in Shenzhen for APEC as Xi and Putin talks loom
weekInBrief.body: President Trump arrived in Shenzhen for the APEC summit, with talks with China’s Xi Jinping and Russia’s Vladimir Putin set for Thursday; trade and limits on advanced AI chips are in focus, days after the U.S. tightened rules on remote access to American AI chips by companies serving Chinese customers.

weekInBrief.headline: Nasdaq slides into correction, down 11% from its high
weekInBrief.body: The Nasdaq is now down 11% from its high, in correction territory, as the AI trade unwinds: Nvidia has fallen for five straight sessions despite its $115.8 billion quarter, software stocks are getting hammered on AI-displacement fears, and traders see a 95.4% chance of a December Fed rate hike.

weekInBrief.headline: Bitcoin sinks toward $62,000, a four-month low
weekInBrief.body: Bitcoin fell about 3.9% to around $62,368, a four-month low, as the risk-off mood spread from stocks into crypto: the token is down roughly 20% since early June, with U.S. spot bitcoin ETF outflows, December rate-hike bets and the Nvidia turmoil all weighing.

weekInBrief.headline: India–U.S. trade deal nearing conclusion
weekInBrief.body: Negotiations on an India–U.S. trade deal are nearing conclusion, with nearly every aspect of the agreement finalised, Commerce Secretary Rajesh Agrawal said Wednesday, though the signing will take some time. A deal would ease tariff pressure on a major U.S. trading partner.

items.headline: Latest from the Strait
items.body: U.S. Central Command widened the blockade on Wednesday, warning that any ship receiving cargo in a ship-to-ship transfer from a vessel loaded at an Iranian port or coastline may be treated as evading the blockade — even if it never enters Iranian waters — and could be stopped, boarded, diverted or seized. CENTCOM spokesman Captain Tim Hawkins said Wednesday that traffic through the strait “continues to flow,” with U.S. forces assisting commercial vessels moving more than 900 million barrels of crude oil through the strait since early May and redirecting more than 100 ships that tried to violate the blockade. On oil, the blockade still holds — Iranian crude exports have remained near a standstill for months, shipping sources told Reuters, while U.S.-escorted non-Iranian crude keeps moving through the strait in the hundreds of millions of barrels.

space.headline: SpaceX catches a Starship returning from orbit — a first
space.body: SpaceX pulled off the first-ever catch of a Starship returning from orbit: the upper stage of Flight 15, launched Friday from Starbase, Texas, circled Earth 14 times, deployed 26 Starlink satellites, then lowered itself into the launch tower’s mechanical arms on Saturday after a 22-hour flight. It was the 15th full-scale Starship flight and only its second trip to orbit. The Super Heavy booster was lost — its engines cut out early and it was diverted to a splashdown in the Gulf of Mexico — so the hoped-for double catch will have to wait. NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman called it “almost magic”; the agency is paying billions for Starship to land Artemis astronauts on the Moon later this decade.

space.headline: An AI that never saw a black hole confirms the M87 ring
space.body: A four-person team at CSIRO, Australia’s national science agency, has independently confirmed the Event Horizon Telescope’s famous 2019 image of the black hole at the centre of galaxy M87. Their method, GenDIReCT, uses a diffusion model trained only on ordinary photographs — landscapes, animals, objects — and rebuilds the image from closure invariants that cancel out telescope calibration errors. It recovered the same glowing ring, 42.2 ± 1.5 microarcseconds across, against the EHT’s 42 ± 3, implying a black hole of 6.5 ± 0.5 billion Suns. The work, published in Nature on Nov. 11, reanalyses the same public EHT data rather than new observations, so it validates the image processing, not the raw measurements.

space.headline: Gravitational waves hint at black holes born from failed supernovae
space.body: Some massive stars may die without a bang, collapsing straight into black holes — and a Caltech-led study of gravitational waves finds hints that such “failed supernovae” really happen. Analysing 257 black-hole mergers recorded by the LIGO–Virgo–KAGRA network over a decade, the team found a dramatic peak at about 10 solar masses — roughly three-quarters of all mergers — and a distinct gap between 12 and 16 solar masses, matching predictions for stars that collapse without exploding. The study, published in Physical Review D on Nov. 10, offers no direct evidence of a failed supernova, only that the data match the prediction.

space.headline: ESA’s Hera flies rectangles around the asteroids DART struck
space.body: ESA’s Hera spacecraft has arrived at the Didymos–Dimorphos asteroid pair — the system NASA’s DART spacecraft deliberately struck in 2022 — and is surveying it from 25–30 km away in “rectangular orbits.” Gravity there is so weak (Didymos pulls about 40,000 times more weakly than Earth) that a normal circular orbit is impractical, so Hera drifts in nearly straight lines at about 12 cm per second, firing thrusters to turn 90 degrees every three to four days. The early characterisation phase runs for about four weeks; next month Hera moves closer, to about 20 km, for bowtie-shaped arcs, with detailed images due Nov. 25.

apod.title: Supernova SN 2026ahvu in NGC 1433
apod.credit: International Gemini Observatory/NOIRLab/NSF/AURA — NASA Image of the Day, November 18, 2026
apod.explanation: A new supernova has been spotted exploding in the spiral galaxy NGC 1433, about 50 million light-years from Earth — and astronomers caught it early. Designated SN 2026ahvu, the Type Ia supernova was discovered on Nov. 2 by the ATLAS survey and is still brightening, expected to peak between Nov. 18 and 23. It is one of the nearest Type Ia supernovae seen since 2011, giving telescopes a rare chance to watch the explosion develop night by night. This before-and-after pair from the Dark Energy Camera shows the galaxy before the blast and with the new supernova shining just below and to the right of its centre.
